plan: Nine new items spreading across less-used SAT types (main purpose, structure with a reversal trap, hypothesis support, modifier placement, paired dashes, its/their, past perfect progressive, cross-text scope, literary inference); S015-01 resubmitted relabelled easy.

passages.title: Kangaroo rats
passages.text: Desert kangaroo rats rarely drink water. Instead, they obtain it from the seeds they eat, partly from the moisture in the seeds and partly from water their bodies produce as they break down food. Their long nasal passages also cool each exhaled breath, so that much of its moisture condenses and is reabsorbed before it can escape.

passages.title: A dim star
passages.text: Astronomers long assumed that a certain dim star appeared faint simply because it was small. A later explanation proposed instead that a thick cloud of dust surrounds the star and blocks much of its light. Measurements of the star's infrared glow, which is produced when dust absorbs starlight and re-emits it as heat, have since supported the dust explanation.

passages.title: Sheep and faces
passages.text: An animal behaviorist hypothesizes that sheep identify familiar people mainly by their faces rather than by other cues, such as voice, clothing, or smell.

passages.title: Rainfall records
passages.text: Having studied the region's rainfall records for more than three decades, ______ that droughts there now last, on average, about twice as long as they did in the 1970s.

passages.title: An inaccurate globe
passages.text: The museum's newest acquisition—a nineteenth-century globe showing several coastlines that later surveys proved inaccurate______ is displayed near the main entrance.

passages.title: A new battery
passages.text: The startup announced that ______ new battery could store nearly twice as much energy as competing designs of the same weight.

passages.title: Waiting hikers
passages.text: By the time the rescue team reached the ridge, the two hikers ______ beneath a rock ledge for nearly two days, rationing the little food they had left.

passages.title: Color words
passages.text:
Text 1
In a famous study, two researchers proposed that languages add basic color words in a predictable order: a word for red appears before a word for green or yellow, and a word for blue comes later still. They based this order on a comparison of nearly one hundred languages.
Text 2
Later linguists noted that most of the languages in that comparison were widely spoken and often written, and that the researchers relied in many cases on a single speaker per language. When these linguists studied languages with fewer speakers in greater depth, several did not follow the proposed order.

passages.title: The speech
passages.text:
The following text is from a short story.
Mara had practiced the speech for three weeks, until she could recite it without looking. When she reached the podium, she set her notes face down, looked out at the rows of folding chairs, and began, instead, to talk about her grandmother.

passages.title: Seven volumes
passages.text: Reviewers called the biographer's account ______: across seven volumes it records nearly every letter the composer wrote, every rehearsal she attended, and every illness she suffered.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that kangaroo rats should be protected from the loss of their desert habitat
choices.B: To describe how kangaroo rats get and conserve water without drinking it
choices.C: To compare the ways kangaroo rats and other desert animals find sources of water
choices.D: To explain why kangaroo rats eat seeds rather than any of the other foods available

candidates.evidence: Their long nasal passages also cool each exhaled breath
candidates.explanation: The text describes two ways kangaroo rats get water (from seeds and from breaking down food) and one way they conserve it (cooling exhaled breath).

A.rationale: The text gives no argument about protection or habitat loss.

D.rationale: The text does not explain their choice of food.

hints: What do all the sentences have in common?

strategy.explanation: State the purpose in your own words first.

candidates.remember: Main purpose covers every sentence, not one detail.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents an early assumption, introduces an alternative explanation, and then reports evidence that favors the original assumption.
choices.B: It describes a set of measurements and then explains why those measurements turned out to be inaccurate.
choices.C: It compares two dim stars and then explains why one of them appears fainter than the other to observers.
choices.D: It presents an early assumption, introduces an alternative explanation, and then reports evidence that favors the alternative.

candidates.evidence: have since supported the dust explanation
candidates.explanation: Sentence 1 gives the early view (small star), sentence 2 the alternative (dust), and sentence 3 evidence (infrared glow) supporting the alternative.

A.rationale: The infrared measurements support the dust explanation, not the original assumption.

B.rationale: The measurements are presented as support, not as errors.

hints: Which explanation do the measurements support?
candidates.remember: Structure questions: watch for choices that reverse which view the evidence supports.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (supporting a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the behaviorist's hypothesis?

choices.A: Sheep trained to approach a familiar handler chose that handler's photograph over strangers' photographs, though no sound or scent was present.
choices.B: Sheep approached a familiar handler more readily when the handler wore the same jacket as during earlier visits than when the handler wore a new one.
choices.C: Sheep in large flocks were found to respond to familiar handlers' voices more quickly than sheep in small flocks responded to those voices.
choices.D: Sheep kept near people for several years approached any human more readily than sheep that had little contact with people did.

candidates.evidence: identify familiar people mainly by their faces
candidates.explanation: Choosing a familiar person's photograph, with voice and smell removed, isolates faces as the cue, which directly supports the hypothesis.

B.rationale: This suggests clothing matters, which the hypothesis says is not the main cue.

C.rationale: This concerns voice, not faces, and compares flock sizes.

D.rationale: Approaching any human does not show recognition of familiar individuals by face.

hints: Which finding rules out the other cues the hypothesis names?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate findings that point to other cues.

candidates.remember: Support for a hypothesis isolates the proposed cause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.B: it was clear to the hydrologist
choices.D: the conclusion of the hydrologist was

candidates.evidence: Having studied the region's rainfall records for more than three decades
candidates.explanation: The person who studied the records must be the subject right after the opening phrase: "the hydrologist concluded."

A.rationale: The opening phrase would describe the records, which cannot study anything.

B.rationale: "It" cannot be the one who studied the records.

D.rationale: A conclusion cannot study rainfall records.

strategy.explanation: The noun after the comma must be the one studying.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier describes the subject that follows it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The phrase beginning "a nineteenth-century globe" interrupts "acquisition ... is displayed" and opens with a dash, so it must close with a dash.

A.rationale: An interruption opened with a dash must close with a dash, not a comma.

C.rationale: A semicolon would separate the subject "acquisition" from its verb "is displayed."

D.rationale: A colon cannot close an interrupting phrase.

hints: How does the interrupting phrase begin?
candidates.remember: Interruptions use matching punctuation on both sides.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The antecedent "the startup" is singular, so the singular possessive "its" is correct.

A.rationale: "Their" is plural, but "the startup" is a single company.

B.rationale: "It's" means "it is," which does not fit before "new battery."

hints: What noun does the pronoun refer to, and is it singular or plural?
candidates.remember: A company is singular: its, not their.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: By the time the rescue team reached the ridge
candidates.explanation: "By the time ... reached" sets a past reference point; an action continuing up to it takes the past perfect progressive.

B.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an action completed before another past event.

C.rationale: The present tense conflicts with the past-tense "reached."

D.rationale: The future perfect does not fit a past event.

hints: Is the sheltering before, during, or after the team's arrival?
candidates.remember: "By the time" + past: use "had been" for the earlier, ongoing action.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the later linguists in Text 2 most likely respond to the proposal in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that every language adds color words in exactly the order the researchers proposed
choices.B: By arguing that the proposed order may not hold for languages that the original comparison underrepresented
choices.C: By claiming that languages with fewer speakers have no basic color words at all
choices.D: By arguing that the original study included too many languages to be analyzed carefully

candidates.evidence: several did not follow the proposed order
candidates.explanation: Text 2 says the original sample favored widely spoken languages and that some smaller languages break the pattern, so the later linguists would question its generality.

A.rationale: Text 2 reports languages that did not follow the proposed order.

C.rationale: Text 2 says these languages did not follow the order, not that they lack color words.

D.rationale: Text 2 criticizes which languages were included and how, not the number.

hints: What do the later linguists criticize about the original sample?
candidates.remember: Cross-text: find whether Text 2 disputes the data, the method, or the scope.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically describes what the text suggests about Mara?

choices.A: She had forgotten her prepared speech and was forced to improvise.
choices.B: She was too nervous to look at the audience while she spoke.
choices.C: She chose in the moment to give a more personal talk than the one she had prepared.
choices.D: She had written her prepared speech entirely about her grandmother.

candidates.evidence: began, instead, to talk about her grandmother
candidates.explanation: She knew the speech by heart but deliberately turned her notes over and spoke about something else: a choice made at the podium.

A.rationale: She practiced until she could recite it without looking; forgetting is not suggested.

B.rationale: She "looked out at the rows of folding chairs" before speaking.

D.rationale: "Instead" shows the grandmother was not the subject of the prepared speech.

hints: What does "instead" tell you about her prepared speech?
candidates.remember: Literary inference: actions reveal choices the text does not state.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: it records nearly every letter the composer wrote
candidates.explanation: An account that covers nearly every letter, rehearsal and illness is thorough to the point of completeness: "exhaustive."

A.rationale: "Laconic" means using very few words, the opposite of a seven-volume account.

C.rationale: A perfunctory account would be hasty and superficial, not one that records nearly everything.

D.rationale: "Tendentious" means biased toward a point of view; nothing in the text describes bias.

hints: What does the colon clause tell you about the account?
candidates.remember: Predict a word from the clause after the colon before reading the choices.
